newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland unveils first 'balanced' budget since 1990.
newsitem.headline: Finland unveils first 'balanced' budget since 1990.

text.p: The 1997 Finnish budget presented to parliament on Tuesday is the country's first since 1990 to balance revenue against spending before debt service payments, finance ministry budget chief Erkki Virtanen said.
"Next year, we need to borrow only to pay interest on old debts," he told a news conference.
The core of the budget is in balance, with state revenue excluding borrowing at the same level as state expenditure excluding debt servicing "for the first time since 1990," Virtanen said.

Income tax reductions worth 5.5 billion markka are expected to help boost private consumption next year. The tax cuts -- suitably timed ahead of local elections in October -- also divert attention from a continued drive to trim expenditure.
"Spending will be about 16 billion markka smaller next year than without the government programme's (savings) decisions," the government said.

"As a whole, annual central government expenditure will be at the end of the election period (in 1999) about 23 billion markka smaller than in a case where savings decisions had not been taken," it added.
Central government spending cuts already implemented since 1991 and those still to come by 1999 will exceed 10 percent in relation to GDP, it said.

Total state spending will fall to 200.4 billion markka in 1997 from 212.9 billion in 1996. Budget spending will be 190.8 billion markka. Due to technical changes, 1997 outlays cannot be compared with earlier years, budget chief Virtanen said. @
"It looks like the (1997) net financing requirement for the state finances will remain below 30 billion markka," he said, adding that figure included items outside the actual budget.
In the budget book, net borrowing is projected at 28.8 billion markka.
This year, net borrowing including items outside the budget and an autumn supplementary budget would be 44.7 billion markka, Virtanen said.
Measured by comparable methods, state debt servicing costs will rise to 31 billion markka next year from 29.3 billion in 1996, he said.

The technical changes caused a 1997 debt servicing figure of 27.09 billion markka for 1996. Regardless of how one measured, it was clear that state debt servicing is the second biggest expenditure category after social and health affairs, Virtanen said.

The decreasing need for new borrowing would gradually bring the steep rise in state indebtedness to a halt, the government said, forecasting state debt to GDP at 71.9 percent in 1997, up from just 10 percent in 1990.
"After 1997 it will start to decline slightly from the level of about 72 percent of GDP," it said.
A new 1996-97 economic forecast also radiated confidence.
"Economic growth is expected to be vigorous in 1997," the finance ministry's economics department said in a statement with the economic projections on which the budget was built.
GDP growth would accelerate to 3.9 percent in 1997 from 2.6 percent this year. Domestic demand would be strong but inflation remain low and the current account show a healthy surplus.

"As a result of the current account surpluses, net foreign debt is on the decrease," the finance ministry said. At end-1997, its ratio to total output would fall to 35 percent from a peak of 54 percent in 1993.
"We have stabilised the economy," Prime Minister Lipponen said. Firms and municipalities should now feel confident about investing, he added.

The government pointed to a fall of nearly three percentage points in long benchmark bond yields since it took office in spring 1995, and said its economic policy targetting EMU entry in the first wave in 1997 would remain on course.
"Finland aims at meeting the convergence criteria of the Economic and Monetary Union so that Finland could participate in the EMU right at the beginning of its third stage in 1999," it said.
The economic scenario outlined by the finance ministry and the balance achieved in the core budget made the outlook bright.
"Finland has good prospects for fulfilling the convergence criteria in 1997," the government said.

"In the future, economic growth can be rapid without a risk of unbalanced price, monetary or foreign trade developments," it said, adding Finnish net foreign debt to GDP would fall further to about 20 percent by the end of the decade.
The only dark cloud was unemployment. The jobless rate "will fall by only one percentage point", the finance ministry said, referring to 1997, from this year's 16.4 percent.
